F00-1: Vivian and the five classmates are fictional characters; the events involving them are adapted from real reports, surveys, or regulations, listed in each year's "What this year's story is based on".
F00-2: Every year's policies, slogans, and amounts are taken from the official or news sources on this page; figures like "NT$10,000," "waitlist 87," and "NT$500 increase" are game settings.
F00-3: The “poster used to block someone” is a dramatized device; what the sources record is who bears the same kind of cost.
F00.title: What is true, what is made up
F01-1: Starting in August 2018, the government started subsidized private preschools, signing contracts to subsidize eligible private preschools.
F01-2: Parents pay no more than NT$4,500 per month.
F01-3: The government requires preschool teachers to be paid at least NT$29,000 per month.
F01.title: Subsidized private preschools launch
F02-1: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU) survey: about 30% of preschool teachers earned less than NT$29,000 per month.
F02-2: Some operators said NT$29,000 includes year-end bonuses and performance bonuses.
F02-3: Ministry of Education responded: NT$29,000 excludes year-end and performance bonuses, with regular audits.
F02-4: PTS reported: NFTU found cases of NT$21,000 monthly pay in Changhua and Chiayi.
F02.title: 30% of preschool teachers paid under NT$29,000
F03-1: In 2019, there were 1,063 subsidized private preschools, offering over 110,000 places.
F03-2: Attending a subsidized private preschool costs NT$4,500 per month.
F03-3: Children over age 2 not in public preschool or subsidized private preschool could receive a childcare allowance of NT$2,500 per month.
F03.title: Subsidized private preschool scale after one year
F04-1: Taipei City public preschools canceled 10 reserved places for 3-year-olds in 2019.
F04-2: At one Zhongshan District public preschool, after the lottery for 5- and 4-year-olds, all 61 3-year-olds were waitlisted.
F04-3: Parents who lost the lottery switched to private preschools, paying over NT$20,000 per month, 5 times the public preschool cost.
F04.title: All 3-year-olds waitlisted
F05-1: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU) survey: local public preschool lottery success rates ranged from 4% to 47%.
F05-2: More than half of places had success rates below 30%.
F05.title: Public preschool odds: 4% to 47%
F06-1: In May 2021 classes were suspended; parents could take "pandemic childcare leave."
F06-2: Employers must approve the leave and must not dock attendance bonuses or treat them unfavorably.
F06-3: The regulations did not require employers to pay.
F06.title: Pandemic childcare leave: approved, unpaid
F08-1: "Niusnews Honest Talk" group survey: 76% did not take pandemic childcare leave, 24% did.
F08-2: Reasons respondents gave: no pay, short staffing, fear of affecting performance and promotion.
F08-3: Someone said: "No one can back up my work."
F08.title: 76% of moms didn't dare take it
F09-1: The government launched the "NT$30 billion central expanded rent subsidy program."
F09-2: After one college student applied, the landlord told every household that because of his application, rent would rise NT$1,000.
F09-3: He said afterward neighbors in the building glared at him and bullied him.
F09.title: Applied for rent subsidy, landlord raised the whole building
F10-1: The NT$30 billion rent subsidy originally planned to subsidize 500,000 households; by end of August 2022 about 278,000 households had applied.
F10-2: One renter said her landlord said: apply and rent will rise at least NT$5,000, so she gave up.
F10-3: Many feared rent hikes or non-renewal after applying.
F10.title: Half did not apply for rent subsidy
F11-1: Academia Sinica survey: about 24.3% of landlord respondents raised rent.
F11-2: Ministry of the Interior responded: comparing application data, rents were flat about 93%, up about 6%.
F11.title: Rent hikes: survey vs government
F12-1: Childcare allowance: NT$3,500 per month starting August 2021.
F12-2: NT$5,000 per month starting August 2022, with more for a 2nd and 3rd child.
F12.title: Childcare allowance to NT$5,000
F13-1: Public preschool after-hours care has had fixed fees since winter break 2024.
F13-2: NT$35 per hour after school on weekdays; NT$2,000 per month during winter and summer breaks.
F13-3: School year 113, 2nd semester: 95.35% of public preschools offered it.
F13-4: The K-12 Education Administration funded 540 extra care staff for school year 114.
F13.title: Public preschool after-hours care: fees and coverage
F14-1: In many counties and cities, public preschool after-hours care runs to 6 p.m., some to 7 p.m.
F14-2: After-hours special-needs student assistants are paid NT$183 per hour, and often no one can be found.
F14-3: In Tainan, some preschools switched to preschool teachers, at the same NT$183 hourly rate.
F14.title: Care till evening, no one to staff it
F15-1: Starting winter break 2024, public preschool care during summer and winter break costs at most NT$2,000 per month.
F15-2: Previously, parents paid out of pocket for public preschool care during summer and winter break, which could cost even more than private preschool.
F15-3: When proposing it, the Tainan City education bureau chief said public preschools must avoid an enrollment disadvantage.
F15.title: Public preschools open in breaks
F16-1: The “Youth Marriage, Childbearing and Rental Assistance Program” starts in 2026.
F16-2: Rental subsidies rise 50% within 2 years of registered marriage, plus another 50% for each additional child.
F16-3: Ministry of the Interior said: "As long as people dare to marry and have children, the government will fully support them."
F16-4: 20% of public housing is reserved for newlywed and child-rearing families; the family housing units allow stays of up to 12 years.
F16.title: “As long as people dare to marry and have children”
F17-1: Starting January 1, 2026, unpaid parental leave can be applied for "by the day," up to 30 days total.
F17-2: During the period, there is still an 80% salary subsidy.
F17-3: The Ministry of Labor's own Q&A asks: coworkers without children must cover the work of employees on flexible unpaid parental leave; will their rights be harmed?
F17-4: Ministry of Labor answers: employers can pay a job-cover allowance; at companies with fewer than 30 people, for 1 day of employee leave the government pays the employer NT$1,000.
F17.title: Parental leave by the day
F18-1: The Executive Yuan's “New Strategy for Taiwan's Population” proposed a first-ever NT$800-a-day “job-cover allowance.”
F18-2: Same plan: parental leave upgraded to "childcare leave," with by-the-day leave increased to 60 days.
F18-3: Same plan: new 0-to-18 growth allowance of NT$5,000 per person per month.
F18.title: First-ever NT$800-a-day job-cover allowance
F19-1: Ministry of Labor plan: when companies let child-rearing employees reduce hours, the government subsidizes wages, and also pays an allowance for hiring cover.
F19-2: The labor minister said he hopes it takes effect in 2027 (ROC year 116).
F19.title: Job-cover allowance timeline
F20-1: Legislative Yuan negotiated amendments to the Act of Gender Equality in Employment and Employment Insurance Act, with no consensus on most articles.
F20-2: Reduced working hours for childcare remains at the current "under age three."
F20-3: Ministry of Labor agreed to expand childcare leave age to under 8, but there is also no consensus on that article.
F20.title: October 2026 childcare law talks
F21-1: The draft Assisted Reproduction Act amendment would include lesbian couples and single women.
F21-2: At the July 16, 2026 committee review, the first review was not completed; another review must be scheduled.
F21.title: Assisted Reproduction Act review
F22-1: In summer 2024, public preschools offered affordable after-hours care for the first time; rural teachers said the subsidy for extra care staff was there on paper but out of reach.
F22-2: Rural public preschool teachers said: one person watches the whole class, can't use the bathroom, doesn't dare drink water, and will get cystitis sooner or later.
F22.src: United Daily News 2024-07-08 (paid article, quoted from opening)
F22.title: One teacher, whole class, no water

ui.title: Sources
F07.title: “The government will be parents’ best teammate”
F07-1: President Tsai Ing-wen said on 2021-05-07: the government will keep being parents’ best teammate.
F07-2: Slogan at the same event: let everyone “be willing to marry, dare to give birth, and enjoy raising children”.
A01.title: Executive Yuan Minister Without Portfolio Lin Wanyi
A01-1: Lin Wanyi: subsidized private preschools cut parents’ cost to no more than NT$4,500 per child per month, solving the polarization in preschool education.
A02.title: Childcare Policy Alliance
A02-1: Childcare Policy Alliance: affirms "real publicization" measures like more nonprofit preschools and public childcare homes; says subsidized private preschools will not fix the messy private market.
A03.title: Taiwan Parents Education Alliance Chair Hsieh Kuo-ching
A03-1: Hsieh Kuo-ching: the 0-to-2 subsidized private childcare subsidy is fairly good, but the government must stop providers from raising prices.
A04.title: National Preschool Education Federation President Ho Ming-te
A04-1: Ho Ming-te: children in private preschools should get at least NT$2,500 per month, and education resources should be evenly distributed.
A05.title: ROC Child Education and Care Federation; ROC Preschool Education Federation
A05-1: Two private preschool associations: "All private preschools nationwide have decided not to join the subsidized private preschool plan," and reported it to the Fair Trade Commission.
A06.title: KMT Legislative Caucus
A06-1: KMT caucus: forcing subsidized private childcare through has created a lose-lose-lose situation; the Executive Yuan should rewrite childcare policy and give operators a fair, competitive environment.
A07.title: Deputy Education Minister Fan Sun-lu
A07-1: Fan Sun-lu: 275 private preschools have joined the subsidized private preschool plan, giving parents more affordable choices.
A08.title: DPP Legislator Chung Chia-pin
A08-1: Chung Chia-pin: the government can "purchase services," with contracted preschools providing places after passing government review.
A09.title: Taipei City Department of Education
A09-1: Taipei City Department of Education: "Public-private cooperation benefits parents and children alike," with 89 preschools joining the subsidized private preschool plan.
A10.title: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU)
A10-1: NFTU: about 30% of preschool teachers earned less than NT$29,000 per month; some providers said NT$29,000 includes year-end and performance bonuses.
A11.title: National Educare Industry Union
A11-1: National Educare Industry Union: higher subsidies have not reached preschool teachers' guaranteed pay; authorities should set up inspection and complaint channels.
A12.title: Childcare Policy Alliance
A12-1: Childcare Policy Alliance: the promise of a "NT$28,000 monthly insured salary" at subsidized private infant-care centers fell apart as soon as the policy launched.
A13.title: Executive Yuan Minister Without Portfolio Lin Wanyi
A13-1: Lin Wanyi: speed up public preschools, adding 2,247 classes and 60,000 public or nonprofit preschool places in 4 years.
A14.title: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU)
A14-1: NFTU: the Ministry of Education should spend more in crowded areas and add public preschools.
A15.title: Childcare Policy Alliance
A15-1: Childcare Policy Alliance: dual-income families should always be able to find nearby, quality, affordable, nonprofit public childcare, with no more lotteries.
A16.title: KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu, Taipei Councilor Chang Szu-kang
A16-1: Lee Yen-hsiu, Chang Szu-kang: Taipei preschools cannot meet demand; rather than large yearly subsidies, use empty school buildings so every district has public childcare and preschools.
A17.title: Taipei Councilor Hsu Shu-hua
A17-1: Hsu Shu-hua: after the 3-year-old classes were cut, of Taipei’s 3,000-plus 3-year-olds, “not one can attend a public preschool.”
A18.title: President Tsai Ing-wen
A18-1: President Tsai Ing-wen: the government will keep being parents’ best teammate, so everyone can “be willing to marry, dare to give birth, and enjoy raising children”.
A19.title: Education Minister Pan Wen-chung
A19-1: Pan Wen-chung: asks employers to support pandemic childcare leave, and to let staff work flexibly from home.
A20.title: Awakening Foundation and other groups (27 in all)
A20-1: Awakening Foundation and 26 other groups: the government should use relief funds to pay an allowance during "pandemic childcare leave," and broaden the reasons for taking it.
A21.title: KMT Legislator Wan Mei-ling
A21-1: Wan Mei-ling: if employers face trouble from granting pandemic childcare leave, the government should also help them.
A22.title: TPP Legislator Lai Hsiang-ling
A22-1: Lai Hsiang-ling: most SMEs lack resources to keep paying wages, and labor-management relations may grow tenser.
A23.title: New Power Party
A23-1: New Power Party: pandemic response should be shared by government, business and labor, not fall on workers alone.
A24.title: Deputy Minister of the Interior Hua Ching-chun
A24-1: Hua Ching-chun: the expanded rent subsidy is a new milestone, to run at NT$30 billion per year in principle.
A25.title: Construction and Planning Agency Housing Division Chief Ou Cheng-hsing
A25-1: Construction and Planning Agency: the NT$30 billion rent subsidy is a four-year plan, "a continuing policy".
A26.title: OURs (Organization of Urban Re-s) (Nest Movement)
A26-1: Nest Movement: the NT$30 billion rent subsidy avoids the black-market rental flaws; the government should focus on "more rental homes" and "clear rental deals".
A27.title: Tsuei Ma Ma Foundation
A27-1: Tsuei Ma Ma Foundation: tenants applying for rent subsidy may face rent hikes, early termination, or non-renewal.
A28.title: New Power Party Legislator Chiu Hsien-chih
A28-1: Chiu Hsien-chih: even after receiving the subsidy, landlords can retaliate with rent hikes.
A29.title: President Tsai Ing-wen (2020 campaign)
A29-1: Tsai Ing-wen: the NT$2,500 monthly childcare allowance will rise to NT$5,000 in four years, “the state will raise the next generation with them”.
A30.title: KMT Vice-Presidential Candidate Chang San-cheng (Han platform)
A30-1: Chang San-cheng (Han Kuo-yu platform): “666” childcare subsidy, NT$60,000 per year regardless of birth order, until age 6.
A31.title: Social and Family Affairs Administration, Ministry of Health and Welfare
A31-1: Ministry of Health and Welfare: in response to parents’ views on different amounts for same-age children, the childcare allowance is raised to NT$5,000.
A32.title: Childcare Policy Alliance
A32-1: Childcare Policy Alliance: raising the childcare allowance is the wrong policy, pushing women home to raise children; the money should fund public childcare.
A33.title: Awakening Foundation
A33-1: Awakening Foundation Secretary-General Chou Yu-hsuan: “throwing money” does not work; more workplace-friendly policies to ease parents’ burdens are needed.
A34.title: New Power Party Legislator Wang Wan-yu
A34-1: Wang Wan-yu: asks counties and cities to raise the share offering after-school care that fits parents’ work hours.
A35.title: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU)
A35-1: NFTU and Wang Wan-yu: public preschools' hours should match subsidized private and nonprofit preschools, and fees should not be higher than subsidized private ones.
A36.title: Childcare and Employment Policy Alliance and civic groups
A36-1: Groups review childcare in six metros: public preschools offer after-hours care, but hours are unstable and do not meet working parents' needs.
A37.title: National Education Union (NEU)
A37-1: NEU: public preschool care runs to 6 p.m., some to 7 p.m.; at NT$183 an hour, no special-education assistants can be found for after hours, so raise that pay first.
A38.title: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU)
A38-1: NFTU: long called for lower preschool teacher-child ratios, more special-education assistants, and after-school care ending no later than 6 p.m.
A39.title: National Preschool Industry Union
A39-1: National Preschool Industry Union: frontline feedback says “teachers work year-round with no rest, really exhausted”; results come at the cost of educators’ overwork.
A40.title: Tainan Education Bureau Director Cheng Hsin-hui
A40-1: Cheng Hsin-hui: public preschool parents pay no more than NT$2,000 per month for break-time care, to keep public enrollment strong.
A41.title: National Educare Industry Union
A41-1: National Educare Industry Union Director Chen Liang-yin: public preschools ending at 4 p.m. with summer and winter breaks still trouble parents; fill the service gap.
A42.title: National Federation of Teachers Unions (NFTU)
A42-1: NFTU: because of after-school care, public preschools ended up costing more than subsidized private ones, "public and private turned upside down."
A44.title: ROC Preschool Education Federation
A44-1: Preschool Education Federation: uneven subsidies push private preschools to the margins; it calls for "equal subsidies."
A45.title: Taichung Preschool Education and Welfare Association
A45-1: Taichung Preschool Education and Welfare Association Chair Ho Jui-chien: calls on the government to raise preschool subsidies for ages 2 to 6 in private preschools.
A46.title: Ministry of the Interior
A46-1: Ministry of the Interior: if people dare to marry and have children, the government will fully support them; 20% of public housing is reserved for newly married and child-raising families.
A47.title: Social Housing Promotion Alliance
A47-1: Social Housing Promotion Alliance: adding married and child-raising families to public housing is worth trying; it also urges quick approval of the 130,000-unit building plan.
A48.title: OURs (Organization of Urban Re-s) Secretary-General Peng Yang-kai
A48-1: Peng Yang-kai: reserving at least 20% of public housing for newly married or families with minor children is fine in direction; the key is overall public housing supply.
A49.title: Tsuei Ma Ma Foundation CEO Lu Ping-yi
A49-1: Lu Ping-yi: with public housing supply cut, not only married and child-raising families, all applicants will see fewer units.
A50.title: Taiwan Youth Association for Democracy
A50.src: Tsuei Ma Ma Foundation (20-group joint release) 2026-05-27
A50-1: Taiwan Youth Association for Democracy Chair Yang Tzu-ying: young people are becoming a “renting generation”; public housing should not be welfare for the disadvantaged, but a public asset that lasts.
A51.title: Taiwan Youth Thought Association and youth groups
A51-1: Taiwan Youth Thought and youth groups: propose 5 review points for housing policy, including more public housing and reasonable rent subsidy amounts.
A52.title: Ministry of Labor
A52-1: Ministry of Labor: “unpaid parental leave by the day, care by the hour; businesses keep talent, the government fully supports”.
A53.title: Childcare and Employment Policy Alliance
A53-1: Childcare and Employment Policy Alliance: using unpaid parental leave by the day is the least disruptive yet most direct approach for all sides.
A54.title: Awakening Foundation
A54-1: Awakening Foundation: affirms the right to take unpaid parental leave by the day to care for infants, but only 30 single days is still not enough.
A55.title: Childcare and Employment Policy Alliance
A55-1: Childcare and Employment Policy Alliance: amend Article 19 of the Gender Equality in Employment Act, with extra pay for covering for a coworker paid by the government.
A56.title: Chinese National Federation of Industries
A56-1: Federation of Industries: counting unpaid parental leave by the day may strain staffing in SMEs; recommends keeping applications by the month.
A57.title: General Chamber of Commerce Chair Hsu Shu-po
A57-1: Hsu Shu-po: splitting unpaid parental leave too finely may affect business operations; recommends using “half-year” or “month” as the unit.

F32-1: Penny takes one day of unpaid parental leave → Ministry of Labor Q&A: Unpaid parental leave can be applied for by the "day," up to 30 days combined; family care leave can be applied for by the "hour"; military, civil service, and teaching personnel are also covered.

F23-1: Parents holding the "NT$4,500 a month" flyer ask Kevin how he can charge NT$10,000 → TVBS 2019-04-16: A mother estimated that public preschool costs just over NT$2,000 per month, while private preschool costs at least NT$15,000 per month.

F24-1: The supervisor says 200 more preschools will join the subsidized private preschool program this year → Rti 2018-09-17: The first wave of private preschools joining the subsidized private preschool program totaled 200, accounting for 26.4% of eligible preschools in non-special-municipality counties and cities nationwide; the Executive Yuan instructed the Ministry of Education to communicate more actively with providers.

F25-3: Amy is waitlist #87 → Business Today 2019-04-10: A mother said enrollment for 3-year-olds is extremely difficult, with waitlists starting in the hundreds.

F27.title: 2022: what this year's story is based on (1)
F28-1: Amy resigns when her parental leave expires → MOHW survey (National Women's Center 2026-06-19): 21.6% of women aged 15 to 64 have left a job for 3 months or more due to marriage, childbirth, or caring for family; those who left due to childcare return to work after about 5 years on average.

F24-2: Jessica actually takes home 26,000 → See "30% of preschool teachers paid under NT$29,000" on this page; "26,000" is a game number.
F25-1: The supervisor says "the Executive Yuan will add 2,247 classes in four years" → Executive Yuan 2018-09-18: Minister without Portfolio Lin Wanyi said 2,247 public or nonprofit preschool classes will be added in the next 4 years.
F26.title: 2021: what this year's story is based on
F26-2: Jason gets other people's work dumped on him → Council of Labor Affairs statistics (cited by PeoPo 2008-01-09): when employees take unpaid parental leave, 33% of companies do not fill the vacancy and directly reassign staff in the same department.
F27-1: Jason's landlord says rent will go up NT$500 next term → See "Applied for rent subsidy, landlord raised the whole building" (NT$1,000 per household) and "Half did not apply" (applying means a raise of at least NT$5,000) on this page; "500" is a game number.
F28-2: HR asks her about her two-year gap → 1111 Job Bank survey (UDN 2026-05-12): 98.6% of respondents think re-entering the workforce is not easy, 52.7% feel significant pressure, and 67.1% think companies become less accepting as age increases.
F29-2: A parent says after-hours care is just what teachers should do → UDN 2025-05-27: frontline teachers often stay until dark, while also enduring parents' complaints and late pickups.
